newsitem.title: USA: US survey shows concern over human rights, trade.
newsitem.headline: US survey shows concern over human rights, trade.

text.p: Most Americans believe the United States should link labour, environmental and human rights issues to international trade but they also believe it would do little good, a survey released on Wednesday said.

The survey, conducted by EPIC/MRA of Lansing, Michigan, for the Association of Women in International Trade, said 67 percent of Americans believe labour, environmental and human rights issues should be linked with trade agreements. But 60 percent believe such an approach will not work to solve those problems, the survey said.

Ed Sarpolus, who conducted the survey, said it showed the more Americans knew about trade and the international economy the more they supported trade. It also showed that people tend to blame trade for economic troubles at home.
"Trade is the new evil empire for the '90's," he said.

The survey showed that the more education and economic security a person had the more he or she tended to be supportive of trade, Sarpolus said. Women over 50 years of age earning less than $45,000 a year were the most critical of international trade, he said.

About 26 percent of those surveyed believed that cheap labour overseas was a major cause of U.S. job loss in the past four years, but less than three percent tied international trade to a personal job loss.

Only about 17 percent of those surveyed believed the United States should pull out of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), which unites the United States, Canada and Mexico in a free trade zone.

About 40 percent believed 50 percent to 90 percent of the cars sold in the United States were made in Japan, Sarpolus said. The Commerce Department's 1995 trade figures show 11.4 percent of cars sold in the United States were made in Japan.

The survey also found that union members and those who supported Texas billionaire Ross Perot, who fought NAFTA, owned about the same number of foreign cars as non-union members and non-Perot supporters. "There is no such thing as a loyalty index," Sarpolus said.
The survey involving 850 Americans in 50 states has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 percent, sponsors said.
